patient.name: Patricia Murray
patient.setting: Orthopaedic ward, day 2 after hip fracture fixation
patient.complaint: Rigors, back pain and low blood pressure 15 minutes into her second unit of blood
background: Dynamic hip screw for a left hip fracture 2 days ago
Post-operative Hb 68 g/L; two units of red cells prescribed
Three pregnancies; transfused once after a postpartum haemorrhage
Blood group O RhD positive; mild heart failure on bisoprolol

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a patient who becomes unwell during or after a transfusion: the timing, BP, JVP, temperature and rash decide which reaction it is.

points: First unit went in overnight without a problem.
Second unit started at 09:00 on a busy ward.
At 09:15 Patricia has **rigors** and **pain in her lower back**.
She feels hot, breathless and frightened.

steps.lead: Patricia is mid-transfusion and has **previous transfusion and pregnancies**: the two risk factors in the notes.
Her BP has fallen to **82/48**. Hypotension during a transfusion means **stop it now**, whatever the cause turns out to be.

visual.title: Patricia's observations during unit 2
visual.caption: Within 15 minutes BP falls and pulse climbs as her temperature reaches 38.9°C. Acute reactions happen early, so obs are repeated at 15 minutes.

steps.q: Fever, rigors, back pain, hypotension and dark urine minutes into a unit. Which reaction?
steps.r: Back pain plus **haemoglobinuria** plus shock within minutes is **ABO-incompatible acute haemolysis**. A febrile non-haemolytic reaction does not drop the BP or darken the urine.

steps.lead: Patricia fits the **acute haemolytic** pattern. Learn the others by their distinguishing feature: rash, wheeze, JVP, hypoxia or a late onset.

steps.title: Telling the reactions apart
head: Reaction
Fever
BP
Key clue
rows: Back pain, dark urine, minutes in
Normal JVP, hypoxia despite O2, within 6 h
Rash, jaundice, pancytopenia, 2 days to 6 weeks

visual.title: Hours after starting the transfusion
bands: 0–6 h: haemolytic, allergic, febrile, TACO, TRALI
visual.label: Patricia 15 min
visual.caption: Almost every reaction appears during or within 6 hours. TA-GvHD is the late one: 2 days to 6 weeks.

steps.text: **Hypotension without fever** plus wheeze or angioedema is **anaphylaxis**, not haemolysis. Hypertension with a raised JVP is **TACO**, not TRALI.

steps.lead: Not Patricia's problem, but know them: room-temperature **platelets** grow skin organisms, and stored red cells leak potassium, causing **hyperkalaemia**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which test confirms haemolysis?' (direct antiglobulin test), 'which results fit?' (low Hb and haptoglobin, high LDH and bilirubin) and ABO compatibility questions.

steps.q: Before any blood test, what is the first thing to do for Patricia?
steps.r: **Stop the transfusion immediately**: it comes before investigations for any suspected reaction.

steps.lead: The nurse clamps the line and keeps the cannula open with saline. **Stopping comes first**, before any test.

points: The bag label says **group A**; Patricia is **group O**.
Unit was meant for the patient in the next bay.
Bag and giving set are sealed and sent to the lab.
Bloods drawn from the other arm.

steps.title: Patricia's haemolysis screen
rows: Blood +++, no red cells on microscopy
steps.text: Low haptoglobin, high LDH and bilirubin, and a positive DAT: intravascular haemolysis.

steps.lead: Patricia's Hb fell despite blood, with every haemolysis marker abnormal and a **positive DAT**. The returned bag confirms the mismatch.

visual.title: Patricia's haptoglobin
visual.label: Patricia <0.1
visual.caption: Haptoglobin mops up free haemoglobin and is used up in intravascular haemolysis.

steps.lead: Patricia is **group O** with anti-A and anti-B in her plasma, so she can receive **only group O** red cells. Group A cells were destroyed.

steps.text: Group **O** red cells are the universal donor; group **AB** patients have no anti-A or anti-B, so they are universal red cell recipients.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': always stop the transfusion first, then match the reaction: IM adrenaline, paracetamol, antihistamine, aggressive fluids, furosemide, or oxygen and ICU.

steps.lead: For Patricia: **stop the transfusion**, then oxygen and IV fluids through a new giving set.
Fever, back pain and hypotension mean **acute haemolysis**: aggressive fluids and close monitoring of vitals and **urine output**.

points: High-flow oxygen; 500 mL crystalloid bolus, repeated.
Hourly urine output via her catheter.
Outreach team and haematologist called; **ICU** review.
Incident reported: a wrong-patient bedside check error.

steps.title: Any suspected transfusion reaction
nodes: Recheck patient ID against the bag
Return bag to lab, report the incident
steps.caption: Stopping always comes first; the type of reaction decides the rest.

steps.lead: Patricia needs the **haemolytic** row. Learn each row as a pair: reaction and its one specific treatment.

steps.title: Specific treatment by reaction
head: Reaction
Treatment
rows: Aggressive oxygenation, ICU, fluids for BP

steps.q: Patricia's neighbour, 85, develops breathlessness, BP 178/96 mmHg and a raised JVP during her third unit. After stopping, what next?
steps.r: Hypertension with raised JVP is **TACO**: offload with **IV furosemide**. A fluid bolus would make it worse.

steps.text: Do not give fluids to TACO or furosemide to TRALI. **JVP and BP** decide: high in TACO, normal JVP and low BP in TRALI.

steps.lead: Patricia's error broke the **ABO compatibility** rules; the **DAT** confirmed the haemolysis.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why ABO mismatch causes intravascular haemolysis, why TRALI is non-cardiogenic oedema, why IgA deficiency causes anaphylaxis, or why febrile reactions happen.

steps.lead: Patricia's **pre-formed IgM anti-A** bound the donor cells within minutes, activating complement and bursting them inside her vessels.

steps.title: ABO mismatch to shock
nodes: Group A cells into a group O patient
Recipient IgM anti-A binds the cells
Fever, hypotension, loin pain, DIC, AKI

o: Free haemoglobin and hypotension injuring the kidney
steps.r: Free haemoglobin is toxic to tubules and hypotension cuts renal perfusion: **AKI** is a feared complication of acute haemolysis.

steps.lead: If Patricia's fever had come from **donor white-cell cytokines** rather than red cell destruction, it would have been a mild febrile reaction.
In TRALI, **donor antibodies**, often in FFP, attack the recipient's leukocytes in the lungs, causing capillary leak.
Patricia's heart failure would make her prone to **TACO**: plain volume overload, cardiogenic oedema, **raised JVP and hypertension**.

visual.title: Chest X-ray: TACO or TRALI
visual.caption: Both give bilateral pulmonary oedema on X-ray. The bedside JVP and BP, not the film, separate cardiogenic TACO from non-cardiogenic TRALI.

steps.lead: Someone with **IgA deficiency** makes anti-IgA antibodies, so IgA in donor plasma can trigger **anaphylaxis**.

mcq.q: What is the single most concerning sign during a transfusion?
mcq.r: **Hypotension** is ominous and means stopping the transfusion immediately.

mcq.q: What causes an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction?
mcq.r: **ABO incompatibility**: the most serious acute reaction.

mcq.q: Which feature points to TACO rather than TRALI?
mcq.r: TACO = overload: **raised JVP, hypertension, S3**. TRALI: normal JVP, hypotension.

mcq.q: Which organisms classically contaminate platelet units?
mcq.r: Platelets are stored at **room temperature**, ideal for skin organisms.

mcq.q: Which patients are most at risk of transfusion-associated GvHD?
mcq.r: **Immunosuppressed** recipients (e.g. Hodgkin's) cannot reject donor lymphocytes.

mcq.q: Which test confirms haemolysis in a suspected haemolytic reaction?
mcq.r: The **DAT (direct Coombs)** is positive in a haemolytic reaction.

mcq.q: A group O patient can receive red cells of which group?
mcq.r: Group O plasma has anti-A and anti-B, so only **group O** red cells are safe.

mcq.q: What is the specific treatment of TACO?
What is the treatment of a febrile non-haemolytic reaction?
Why does IgA deficiency predispose to anaphylaxis with transfusion?
o: Anti-IgA antibodies react with donor IgA
mcq.r: The recipient makes **anti-IgA antibodies** that react with IgA in donor plasma.

prompts.q: What are transfusion reactions, their risk factors, and the most concerning sign?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: hypotension during a transfusion means stop now.

points.p: Adverse immune or non-immune responses during or after transfusion
points.why: Some are minutes in, GvHD is weeks later.

points.p: Risk factors: previous transfusion, pregnancy
points.why: Both sensitise the recipient to foreign antigens.

points.p: Hypotension is the most concerning sign: stop immediately

prompts.q: How does an acute haemolytic reaction present and what causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: back pain plus dark urine minutes into a unit.

points.p: Caused by ABO incompatibility
Fever, rigors
Back or loin pain, abdominal pain
Haemoglobinuria (dark urine)
Hypotension and breathlessness
points.why: Can progress to DIC and AKI.

prompts.q: How do you tell TACO from TRALI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: check the JVP and the BP.

points.p: TACO: breathless, hypertension, raised JVP, S3, no fever
TRALI: breathless, hypotension, normal JVP, hypoxia unresponsive to oxygen
TRALI occurs within 6 hours, often linked to FFP

prompts.q: How do febrile non-haemolytic, minor allergic and anaphylactic reactions differ?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fever with stable obs is mild; low BP without fever plus wheeze is anaphylaxis.

points.p: Febrile non-haemolytic: fever and chills, common and mild
Minor allergic: urticarial rash only
Anaphylaxis: angioedema, wheeze, hypotension without fever, urticaria
IgA deficiency is the key risk factor for anaphylaxis

prompts.q: What is transfusion-associated GvHD and what are the other complications of transfusion?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: late rash, jaundice and pancytopenia in an immunosuppressed patient.

points.p: TA-GvHD: fever, rash, jaundice, pancytopenia
2 days to 6 weeks after transfusion, in immunosuppressed or Hodgkin's patients
Bacterial contamination of platelets: Staph epidermidis, Bacillus cereus
Hyperkalaemia from packed red cells

prompts.q: What investigations confirm a haemolytic reaction and what do they show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the DAT is the confirmatory test.

points.p: Stop the transfusion first, before investigations
Haemolysis screen: low Hb, raised LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin
points.why: Haptoglobin is used up binding free Hb.

points.p: Positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test
Cultures if septic; return the bag to the lab to recheck compatibility

prompts.q: Which red cell groups can each ABO group receive?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: O is the universal red cell donor.

points.p: Group O red cells are compatible with everyone
points.why: O cells carry no A or B antigen.

points.p: A receives A (or O); B receives B (or O)
points.why: Each group has antibodies to the antigen it lacks.

points.p: AB patients: AB blood (per the notes)
points.why: AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B.

prompts.q: What is the first step for any reaction, and the management of acute haemolysis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: stop, then fluids and urine output.

points.p: Stop the transfusion immediately
Supportive: oxygen and IV fluids
Aggressive IV fluids, consider ICU
Monitor vitals and urine output closely

prompts.q: What is the specific treatment for each other reaction type?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match reaction to one drug.

points.p: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline, plus steroid and bronchodilator
points.why: IM, not IV, on the ward.

points.p: Febrile non-haemolytic: paracetamol
Minor allergic: pause and give antihistamine
TACO: IV furosemide
TRALI: aggressive oxygenation, ICU, fluids for BP

prompts.q: Why does ABO incompatibility cause such a severe reaction?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: IgM plus complement equals intravascular haemolysis.

points.p: Pre-formed IgM antibodies bind donor red cell antigens
Complement activation causes intravascular haemolysis
Free haemoglobin and mediators: fever, hypotension, loin pain, DIC, AKI

prompts.q: What is the mechanism of TRALI, TACO, febrile and IgA-related reactions?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: TRALI is donor antibodies; TACO is plain volume.

points.p: TRALI: donor antibodies (often FFP) against recipient leukocytes, neutrophil activation, capillary leak
TACO: volume overload, cardiogenic oedema, worse with cardiac or renal impairment
Febrile: cytokines from donor white cells
IgA deficiency: anti-IgA antibodies react with donor IgA

glossary.ABO incompatibility: Transfusion of red cells carrying A or B antigens that the recipient has antibodies against.
glossary.Acute haemolytic reaction: Rapid destruction of transfused red cells, usually from ABO mismatch; the most serious acute reaction.
glossary.Febrile non-haemolytic reaction: Common, mild fever and chills during transfusion caused by cytokines from donor white cells.
glossary.Anaphylaxis: Severe, life-threatening allergic reaction with airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
glossary.Angioedema: Swelling of the deeper skin layers, often lips, tongue and face.
glossary.Urticaria: Itchy, raised wheals (hives) on the skin.
glossary.TACO: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload: pulmonary oedema from too much volume, with raised JVP and hypertension.
glossary.TRALI: Transfusion-related acute lung injury: non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6 hours, often after FFP.
glossary.TA-GvHD: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease: donor lymphocytes attack the recipient, causing rash, jaundice and pancytopenia.
glossary.GvHD: Graft-versus-host disease: donor immune cells attacking the recipient's tissues.
glossary.Pancytopenia: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together.
glossary.Haemoglobinuria: Free haemoglobin in the urine, making it dark red or brown.
glossary.Intravascular haemolysis: Red cells bursting inside the blood vessels, releasing free haemoglobin.
glossary.Haptoglobin: Plasma protein that binds free haemoglobin; it falls in intravascular haemolysis.
glossary.LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase, an enzyme released from damaged cells; raised in haemolysis.
glossary.DAT: Direct antiglobulin test: detects antibody or complement on red cells; positive in immune haemolysis.
glossary.Coombs test: Another name for the antiglobulin test.
glossary.IgM: Large pentameric antibody that fixes complement strongly; anti-A and anti-B are mainly IgM.
glossary.Complement: Plasma proteins that, once activated, punch holes in cell membranes and drive inflammation.
glossary.IgA deficiency: Absence of IgA antibody; recipients may make anti-IgA and react to donor plasma.
glossary.FFP: Fresh frozen plasma, rich in clotting factors and donor antibodies.
glossary.JVP: Jugular venous pressure; raised in fluid overload.
glossary.S3: Third heart sound, heard in volume overload and heart failure.
glossary.Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lungs from leaky capillaries rather than a failing heart.
glossary.Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lungs from raised pressure in an overloaded or failing heart.
glossary.DIC: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: widespread clotting that uses up factors and causes bleeding.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a rapid fall in kidney function.
glossary.Hyperkalaemia: High blood potassium; stored red cells leak potassium.
glossary.Staph epidermidis: Skin commensal that can contaminate room-temperature platelet units.
glossary.Bacillus cereus: Spore-forming bacterium that can contaminate platelet units.
glossary.Furosemide: Loop diuretic used to offload fluid in TACO.
glossary.IM adrenaline: Intramuscular adrenaline, first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
glossary.Universal donor: Group O red cells, which lack A and B antigens.
glossary.Rigors: Violent shaking with chills, often as the temperature rises.

technique.stem: A 68 year old man has a right hemicolectomy and needs a red cell transfusion for blood loss. Ten minutes into the second unit he develops rigors and lower back pain. The urine in his catheter becomes dark. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question during a transfusion: match the features to one reaction.

clues: Ten minutes into the second unit
urine in his catheter becomes dark
steps.x: Minutes in, back pain, haemoglobinuria, fever and shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute haemolytic reaction** from ABO incompatibility.

elim: Anaphylaxis gives hypotension without fever, with wheeze or angioedema.
Febrile non-haemolytic reactions do not drop the BP or cause dark urine.
TACO causes hypertension and a raised JVP.
TRALI causes severe hypoxia, not back pain and haemoglobinuria.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: back pain + dark urine + shock minutes in = ABO haemolysis.

technique.stem: A 55 year old woman develops fever, loin pain and hypotension 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion. The transfusion is stopped. The haematologist wants to confirm whether red cell destruction is taking place.
technique.q: Which set of results is most likely?
o: High haptoglobin, high LDH, low bilirubin
Low haptoglobin, high LDH, high bilirubin
Low haptoglobin, low LDH, normal bilirubin
Normal haptoglobin, normal LDH, high bilirubin
Normal haptoglobin, high LDH, low bilirubin

steps.x: Which haemolysis screen fits an acute haemolytic reaction?

clues: 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion
steps.x: Classic intravascular haemolysis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Haptoglobin used up (**low**), LDH released (**high**), bilirubin from Hb breakdown (**high**), plus a positive DAT.

elim: Haptoglobin falls, and bilirubin rises, in haemolysis.
LDH rises as cells burst.
Haptoglobin and LDH would both be abnormal.
Haptoglobin falls and bilirubin rises.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: haemolysis = low haptoglobin, high LDH, high bilirubin, positive DAT.

technique.stem: A 42 year old woman with sickle cell disease is having a red cell transfusion. After 30 minutes she develops an itchy raised rash on her arms and chest. She has no wheeze, no lip or tongue swelling and no breathlessness. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Continue the transfusion and give IV furosemide
Pause the transfusion and give an antihistamine
Stop the transfusion and give aggressive IV fluids

steps.x: Initial management: first identify which reaction.

clues: no wheeze, no lip or tongue swelling
steps.x: Urticaria only, stable obs, no fever: **minor allergic reaction**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Halt the transfusion and give an antihistamine** (chlorphenamine).

elim: Furosemide is for TACO.
A reaction always means halting the transfusion first.
IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis: no airway, breathing or BP compromise.
Aggressive fluids are for acute haemolysis.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: rash alone = minor allergic = halt plus antihistamine.

technique.stem: A 79 year old woman with blood group O is given a unit of group A red cells in error. Within minutes she has fever, loin pain, hypotension and dark urine. A positive direct antiglobulin test is found.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her red cell destruction?
o: Pre-formed recipient IgG causing delayed extravascular haemolysis

steps.x: Mechanism of acute ABO haemolysis.
Group O plasma has anti-A; minutes means pre-formed antibody; dark urine means intravascular lysis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pre-formed IgM** anti-A binds donor cells and activates **complement**: intravascular haemolysis.

elim: That is TRALI.
That is transfusion-associated GvHD.
IgG causes delayed, extravascular haemolysis days later.
That is TACO.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: ABO = IgM + complement = intravascular haemolysis.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has a postpartum haemorrhage and is transfused red cells. Fifteen minutes into the first unit she feels anxious and has pain in her back and abdomen. Her catheter urine turns dark brown. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, BP 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Back and abdominal pain, haemoglobinuria, fever and shock minutes into a unit, with low haptoglobin and high LDH, are an acute haemolytic reaction. Anaphylaxis occurs without fever.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a reaction during transfusion.

clues: Fifteen minutes into the first unit
pain in her back and abdomen
steps.x: Early, loin pain, dark urine, fever, shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute haemolytic reaction.**

elim: Amniotic fluid embolism happens during labour, with collapse and DIC, not dark urine 15 minutes into a unit.
Anaphylaxis gives hypotension without fever and with wheeze or angioedema.
Febrile reactions keep a normal BP.
TRALI causes severe hypoxia, not haemolysis markers.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: haemolysis markers + loin pain = ABO incompatibility.

practice.stem: An 86 year old man with heart failure and chronic kidney disease is given three units of red cells over 6 hours for anaemia. During the third unit he becomes breathless. He has bibasal crackles, a raised JVP and a third heart sound. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 182/98 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Breathlessness with hypertension, raised JVP and an S3 and no fever is TACO, from volume overload in a patient with cardiac and renal impairment. TRALI has a normal JVP and hypotension.

steps.x: Which reaction? Look at JVP and BP.

clues: heart failure and chronic kidney disease
three units of red cells over 6 hours
steps.x: Volume in, a heart that cannot cope, overload signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **TACO.**

elim: No fever, back pain or dark urine.
Anaphylaxis causes hypotension, not hypertension.
No fever.
TRALI has a normal JVP and hypotension.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: high BP + high JVP + S3 = TACO.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman with liver disease is given fresh frozen plasma before a procedure. Three hours later she becomes acutely breathless. Her JVP is not raised and heart sounds are normal. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg and oxygen saturation 82% on 15 L/min oxygen. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral diffuse airspace shadowing; heart size normal.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Hypoxia refractory to oxygen, hypotension, a normal JVP and bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours of FFP is TRALI. TACO would give hypertension and a raised JVP.

steps.x: Diagnosis: breathless after plasma.
FFP, within 6 hours, normal JVP, hypotension, hypoxia despite oxygen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **TRALI.**

elim: No back pain or haemoglobinuria; FFP contains no red cells.
No wheeze, angioedema or urticaria.
Contamination causes high fever and septic shock, not isolated lung injury.
TACO has a raised JVP and hypertension.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: FFP + hypoxia + normal JVP + low BP within 6 h = TRALI.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man with myelodysplasia, who has had many previous transfusions, is having a unit of red cells. After 45 minutes he feels cold and shivery. He has no rash, wheeze, back pain or breathlessness. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A mild fever with chills and stable observations in a multiply transfused patient is a febrile non-haemolytic reaction, caused by cytokines from donor white cells. Haemolysis would bring hypotension and back pain.

steps.x: Which reaction, with fever but stable obs?

clues: no rash, wheeze, back pain or breathlessness
steps.x: Isolated fever and chills, normal BP, sensitised patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Febrile non-haemolytic reaction.**

elim: No hypotension, back pain or dark urine.
No urticaria.
GvHD is days to weeks later, with rash and jaundice.
No hypoxia or breathlessness.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: fever + chills + normal BP = febrile non-haemolytic.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man with recurrent sinus and chest infections is transfused after a road traffic collision. Within 5 minutes he develops wheeze, lip swelling and widespread hives. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 132 bpm, BP 72/40 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of this reaction?
practice.e: Anaphylaxis (wheeze, angioedema, hypotension without fever) in a man with recurrent sinopulmonary infections points to IgA deficiency, the key risk factor for anaphylactic transfusion reactions.

steps.x: Underlying cause: first name the reaction, then its risk factor.

clues: wheeze, lip swelling and widespread hives
steps.x: Anaphylaxis without fever; recurrent mucosal infections hint at IgA deficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IgA deficiency**, with anti-IgA antibodies.

elim: ABO haemolysis causes fever, loin pain and dark urine.
Contamination causes high fever and rigors, not angioedema.
That is TRALI: hypoxia, not hives and angioedema.
Overload causes hypertension and raised JVP.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: transfusion anaphylaxis = think IgA deficiency.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man is having chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. Two weeks after a red cell transfusion he develops fever, a widespread red rash, diarrhoea and yellow sclera. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, rash, jaundice and pancytopenia 2 days to 6 weeks after transfusion in an immunosuppressed Hodgkin patient is transfusion-associated GvHD. The other reactions occur during or within hours of the transfusion.

steps.x: Diagnosis: note the timing.

clues: Two weeks after a red cell transfusion
steps.x: Immunosuppressed, late onset, rash, jaundice, pancytopenia on bloods.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transfusion-associated GvHD.**

elim: Haemolysis is within minutes and does not cause rash or pancytopenia.
Contamination causes fever during or soon after the unit.
Febrile reactions are during the transfusion and mild.
TRALI is within 6 hours, with hypoxia.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: weeks later + rash + jaundice + pancytopenia in Hodgkin's = TA-GvHD.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man develops fever, back pain and hypotension 10 minutes into a red cell transfusion. The transfusion is stopped and IV fluids are started. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm immune haemolysis?
practice.e: The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test detects antibody on red cells and is positive in a haemolytic transfusion reaction. A blood film or reticulocyte count shows haemolysis but not its immune cause.

steps.x: Confirmatory test for immune haemolysis.

clues: 10 minutes into a red cell transfusion
steps.x: Acute haemolytic reaction; markers already suggest haemolysis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Direct antiglobulin test.**

elim: A film can show spherocytes but does not prove antibody coating.
Ferritin assesses iron stores.
Reticulocytes rise later and are non-specific.
IgA level is for suspected anaphylaxis.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: confirm transfusion haemolysis with the DAT.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman with major bleeding needs urgent red cells. Her blood group is A RhD positive. The only red cell units immediately available in the fridge are listed below. Her temperature is 36.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which red cell group is ABO compatible for this patient?
practice.e: A group A patient has anti-B, so she can receive A or O red cells. Of those available, only group O is compatible. AB and B cells carry the B antigen.

steps.x: ABO compatibility for red cells.

clues: Her blood group is A RhD positive
only red cell units immediately available
steps.x: Group A plasma contains anti-B.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: She can have A or O; only O is available: **O only**.

elim: AB cells carry B antigen.
Both carry B antigen.
B cells would be haemolysed by her anti-B.
AB is incompatible.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: group O red cells are compatible with everyone.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman is 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion on the ward. She suddenly feels unwell with rigors. The nurse calls you. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Hypotension during a transfusion is ominous: stop the transfusion immediately, before investigations or specific treatment. Paracetamol and continuing would be dangerous here.

steps.x: Initial management of a reaction.

clues: 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion
steps.x: Hypotension during transfusion: the most concerning sign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stop the transfusion immediately.**

elim: No features of anaphylaxis; and stopping comes first.
Furosemide is for TACO with hypertension.
Never continue with hypotension.
Slowing still gives more incompatible blood.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: any reaction with low BP = stop first.

practice.stem: An 82 year old man with ischaemic heart disease is on his second unit of red cells. He becomes breathless with bibasal crackles and a raised JVP. The transfusion has been stopped and he is sat upright on oxygen. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 176/94 mmHg and oxygen saturation 91% on 4 L/min oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Hypertension, raised JVP and crackles during transfusion is TACO, treated with IV furosemide. A fluid bolus would worsen the overload.

steps.x: Next step, after stopping and oxygen.
Overload in a weak heart, no fever: TACO.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV furosemide.**

elim: No anaphylaxis: BP is high.
No urticaria.
Fluid worsens overload.
Steroids are adjuncts for anaphylaxis.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: TACO = furosemide.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman is 10 minutes into a red cell transfusion when she develops wheeze, swelling of her lips and tongue, and an urticarial rash. The transfusion has been stopped. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 136 bpm, BP 74/42 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: Wheeze, angioedema and hypotension without fever is anaphylaxis: give IM adrenaline, with steroid, bronchodilator and supportive care. An antihistamine alone is for minor allergic reactions.

steps.x: Next step after stopping: name the reaction.

clues: swelling of her lips and tongue
steps.x: Airway, breathing and circulation compromise, no fever: **anaphylaxis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IM adrenaline.**

elim: Furosemide is for TACO.
An antihistamine alone is for a minor rash only.
Paracetamol is for febrile reactions.
Never restart after anaphylaxis.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: transfusion anaphylaxis = IM adrenaline.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man receives fresh frozen plasma from a multiparous female donor. Two hours later he has severe hypoxaemia unresponsive to oxygen, hypotension and a normal JVP. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates with a normal heart size. His pulse rate is 120 bpm and BP 86/52 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his lung injury?
o: Anti-IgA antibodies reacting with donor IgA
Donor antibodies reacting with recipient leukocyte antigens
Donor lymphocytes attacking recipient lung tissue
Recipient IgM activating complement against donor red cells
Volume overload raising pulmonary venous pressure
practice.e: TRALI: donor antibodies (often in FFP, especially from multiparous donors) react with recipient leukocyte antigens, activating neutrophils and causing capillary leak and non-cardiogenic oedema.

steps.x: Mechanism of lung injury after plasma.
TRALI: plasma from a sensitised donor, within 6 hours, non-cardiogenic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Donor antibodies** against recipient **leukocytes** cause neutrophil activation and capillary leak.

elim: That is anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency.
That is transfusion-associated GvHD, weeks later.
That is ABO haemolysis; FFP has no red cells.
That is TACO, with a raised JVP.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: TRALI = donor antibody vs recipient white cells = leaky lung capillaries.
